title: A star-confined screen fails the 2023 ASASSN-14ko X-ray duration test in a bounded Kepler model
abstract: Can an opaque screen carried near the surviving star make the long 2023 X-ray dip of ASASSN-14ko? We measure the total 0.2-0.5 keV rates in the published XMM-Newton 2-ks table. All 21 faint-state visits stay below 10 percent of the pre-dip rate under a stated Gaussian error test, without a fitted floor. Low samples span at least 32.52 observer days. We derive an exact Kepler bound on the time a screen confined within r(m/M)^(1/3) of a star can block the central ray. This cap is 1.442 times the instantaneous circular Hill radius. We allow any viewing angle and apocentre phase. For black-hole masses 10^6.5-10^8 solar masses, stellar masses 0.1-10 solar masses, stated ordinary-star radius lower bounds, closest approach at least half the tidal radius, and one 108.44-day orbit per dip, a continuous analytic bound is 16.139 days. A generous light-path allowance raises it to 18.594 days, still below the measured span. A solar star at a 10^7-solar-mass black hole needs a screen at least 5.05 times the enlarged cap. This excludes the stated compact screen model, not detached debris or intrinsic shutdown. A doubled orbital period can evade the test. Compact cores, deeper passages and relativistic orbits are outside the proved scope. Code, proof, source hashes, synthetic results and figures are supplied; external record-level data stay outside the package.

display.caption: Low XMM-Newton samples span at least 32.52 days. The tested star-confined screen permits less than 18.60 days, including a generous light-path allowance. This is an exclusion only under the stated size, orbit and stellar bounds.

Inverse constraints after the full light-path allowance. The left panel gives the largest pericentre that can produce the span in the Kepler model. The right panel gives the required screen size relative to the enlarged confinement cap. Values near or below the horizon scale are model failures, not physical orbit estimates.
